title: Do As I Can, Not As I Say: Grounding Language in Robotic Affordances
tldr: An LLM knows how to clean a spill but not whether this robot can. Multiply the language score by a learned value function and you get a plan the body can execute.

problem.task: Execute a long-horizon natural-language instruction by selecting a sequence of learned skills.

inputs.name: instruction
inputs.chars: High-level and temporally extended: "I spilled my drink, can you help?"

inputs.name: observation
inputs.chars: Robot camera, used by the value functions.

outputs.name: next skill
outputs.chars: Argmax of p_LLM(skill | ℓ) × p_affordance(success | o_t, skill).

training.supervision: Skill policies and their value functions trained separately. The LLM is frozen.
training.note: The value function is the grounding — it is what keeps the plan inside what the body can currently do.

method.intuition: A language model supplies what is useful and a value function supplies what is possible. Neither alone yields an executable plan.

datasets.name: real kitchen and office tasks on a mobile manipulator

experiments.headline: Long-horizon abstract instructions completed on a real robot, with affordance grounding shown to be necessary rather than helpful.

why: The paper that established language as the interface layer between semantic knowledge and physical capability.

title: Inner Monologue: Embodied Reasoning through Planning with Language Models
tldr: Feed the outcome back to the planner as text: success detection, scene description, a person's correction. Closed-loop replanning falls out with no extra training.

problem.task: Closed-loop language planning where environment and human feedback re-enter the prompt.

inputs.name: feedback
inputs.chars: Success detector output, scene description, or a person saying "no, the other one" — all as text.

training.supervision: None — the LLM is frozen and everything happens in the prompt.
training.note: Turning heterogeneous feedback into a single text channel is the trick that makes closed-loop control prompt-shaped.

method.intuition: If every kind of feedback is rendered as language, the planner needs no new machinery to close the loop. It just keeps reading.

datasets.name: real tabletop and kitchen mobile manipulation

experiments.headline: Closed-loop language feedback significantly improves high-level instruction completion in three domains, including real-world long-horizon mobile manipulation.

why: The reference implementation of closing the loop through language — the pattern most agent systems on this list inherit.

title: Code as Policies: Language Model Programs for Embodied Control
tldr: The policy is a Python program the LLM writes, so control flow, arithmetic and third-party libraries come for free.

problem.task: Turn a natural-language command into executable robot policy code.

inputs.name: command
inputs.chars: Includes vague terms — "faster", "a bit to the left".

inputs.name: API surface
inputs.chars: Object detectors and control APIs, exposed as callable functions.

outputs.name: policy program
outputs.chars: Python: loops, conditionals, NumPy and Shapely calls, waypoints.

training.note: Hierarchical code-gen — recursively defining undefined functions — is what lets one prompt cover a long tail of commands.

method.intuition: Robot policies already look like programs, so the natural output format for a code-trained LLM is the policy itself rather than a plan to be interpreted.
components: perception and control APIs as first-class functions

datasets.name: multiple real robot platforms and tabletop tasks

experiments.headline: Spatial-geometric reasoning, generalization to unseen instructions, and precise values assigned to vague terms from context.

why: The symbolic branch of robot decision-making: the plan is a program, so it can be inspected, composed and debugged.

title: VoxPoser: Composable 3D Value Maps for Robotic Manipulation with Language Models
tldr: Have the LLM write code that paints affordance and constraint into a 3D voxel grid, then plan a dense trajectory through it — no motion primitives.

problem.task: Zero-shot synthesis of dense 6-DoF end-effector trajectories from open-set language over open-set objects.

inputs.name: RGB-D observation
inputs.chars: Grounded through a VLM into the voxel grid.

training.supervision: None for the base system. An optional online dynamics model is fit from experience for contact-rich scenes.
training.note: The value map is the interface: language decides what it contains, planning consumes it.

method.intuition: LLMs can name affordances and constraints but not act on them. Writing them into a 3D field turns semantics into an objective a planner can optimize.
method.backbone: LLM code generation + VLM grounding + model-based planner

datasets.name: simulated and real everyday manipulation tasks

experiments.headline: A large study across simulation and real robots on open-set instructions and objects, with trajectories that hold up under perturbation during execution.

why: The clearest bridge between the modeling arc and the change arc: the world representation is literally the planning objective.

title: Diffusion Policy: Visuomotor Policy Learning via Action Diffusion
tldr: Human demonstrations are multimodal, because there are several right ways to do a task. A denoising diffusion policy keeps that where a regression head averages it away.

problem.task: Visuomotor imitation: observations to a chunk of future actions.

inputs.name: observation history
inputs.chars: A short window of camera frames plus proprioception.

outputs.name: action chunk
outputs.chars: Denoised over K Langevin steps; executed under receding horizon control.

training.supervision: Behavior cloning from human teleoperated demonstrations.
training.note: Predicting a chunk rather than a single action is what gives temporal consistency. The diffusion head is what preserves multimodality.

method.intuition: Learn the gradient of the action distribution rather than its mean, and the policy stops collapsing between valid strategies.

experiments.headline: Average 46.9% improvement over prior state-of-the-art across 12 tasks and 4 benchmarks.

why: The action representation that reset robot imitation learning, and the head that most later VLAs adopted.

title: Learning Fine-Grained Bimanual Manipulation with Low-Cost Hardware
tldr: Action chunking absorbs compounding error, which is why low-cost imprecise hardware can slot a battery with ten minutes of demonstrations.

problem.task: End-to-end bimanual imitation learning from teleoperated demonstrations on low-cost arms.

inputs.name: multi-camera images + joint positions
inputs.chars: No depth, no calibration, no force sensing.

outputs.name: action chunk
outputs.chars: 14-DoF bimanual joint targets, temporally ensembled across overlapping chunks.

training.supervision: Behavior cloning from about 10 minutes of demonstrations per task, collected through a custom teleoperation rig.
training.note: The CVAE latent absorbs demonstrator non-stationarity, which is the other half of why so little data suffices.

method.intuition: Errors compound because the policy re-decides every timestep. Committing to a chunk of actions cuts the effective horizon by an order of magnitude.

experiments.headline: 80–90% success on tasks like opening a translucent condiment cup and slotting a battery, from 10 minutes of demonstrations each.

why: Made dexterous imitation reproducible outside well-funded labs, which is why so much of the field's data now exists.

title: RT-2: Vision-Language-Action Models Transfer Web Knowledge to Robotic Control
tldr: Write actions as text tokens and co-train a VLM on robot trajectories and web VQA, and web semantics leak into the gripper.

problem.task: End-to-end language-conditioned manipulation from a vision-language backbone.

inputs.name: instruction
inputs.chars: May reference concepts absent from all robot data.

outputs.name: action tokens
outputs.chars: 7-DoF end-effector delta plus gripper, emitted as a string.

training.supervision: Co-fine-tuning on robot trajectories and internet-scale vision-language tasks, in one token stream.
training.note: The recipe is the contribution: one format for both data sources means no architectural bridge is needed.

method.intuition: If actions are text, then robot control is just another vision-language task, and web pretraining stops being a separate stage.
components: co-fine-tuning on web and robot data

metrics: success on seen and unseen objects, backgrounds, instructions
experiments.headline: Large gains on unseen objects and on commands absent from robot training data, including rudimentary reasoning chains.

why: The origin of the VLA category and the reason "pretrain on the web, act in the world" became the default recipe.

title: OpenVLA: An Open-Source Vision-Language-Action Model
tldr: 7B open VLA on 970k real demonstrations that beats a 55B closed model, plus the fine-tuning recipes that make VLAs actually adoptable.

problem.task: Open generalist manipulation policy, fine-tunable to new robots and tasks.

inputs.name: image
inputs.chars: Encoded by fused DINOv2 + SigLIP features.

outputs.name: action tokens
outputs.chars: Discretized 7-DoF, decoded from the LM head.

training.supervision: 970k real robot demonstrations from the Open X-Embodiment collection.
training.note: The fine-tuning study — LoRA, quantization, compute budgets — is what turned VLAs from a demo into infrastructure.

method.intuition: The bottleneck for VLAs was access, not capability: an open model plus an efficient adaptation recipe unblocks everyone else.

experiments.headline: +16.5% absolute over RT-2-X with 7× fewer parameters across 29 tasks, and +20.4% over from-scratch Diffusion Policy after fine-tuning.

why: The open baseline everything in the VLA line is now measured against.

title: π₀: A Vision-Language-Action Flow Model for General Robot Control
tldr: Swap discrete action tokens for a flow-matching head on top of a VLM, and one policy folds laundry, clears tables and assembles boxes across single-arm, dual-arm and mobile platforms.

problem.task: Generalist dexterous control across heterogeneous robot platforms, at high control frequency.

inputs.name: camera images
inputs.chars: Multiple views depending on the platform.

inputs.name: instruction
inputs.chars: From a person or from a high-level VLM policy.

outputs.name: continuous action chunk
outputs.chars: Continuous — flow matching, not discretization — at up to 50 Hz.

training.supervision: Pretraining on a large multi-platform dexterous dataset, then task-specific fine-tuning.
training.note: The pretrain-then-specialize split mirrors language models and is the paper's organizing claim.

method.intuition: Discretizing actions throws away the precision dexterous tasks need. Flow matching keeps them continuous while inheriting the VLM's semantics.

datasets.name: laundry folding, table cleaning, box assembly

experiments.headline: Zero-shot competence after pretraining, language following from people and from a high-level VLM, and new skills acquired by fine-tuning.

why: The current reference point for what a robot foundation model looks like, and the flow-matching head is now standard.

title: GR00T N1: An Open Foundation Model for Generalist Humanoid Robots
tldr: A slow VLM that reasons and a fast diffusion transformer that moves, trained end-to-end together, fed by robot trajectories plus human video plus synthetic data.

problem.task: Generalist humanoid control across embodiments, language-conditioned.

training.supervision: Heterogeneous mixture: real robot trajectories, human videos, synthetic generated data. Both systems trained jointly end to end.
training.note: The data mixture is the interesting variable — human video and synthetic data are treated as first-class, not as auxiliary.

method.intuition: Semantic interpretation and motor control run at different timescales, so give them different modules but train them as one model so the interface is learned rather than designed.
components: heterogeneous data mixture including human video

datasets.name: real robot trajectories + human video + synthetic data

experiments.headline: Outperforms imitation-learning baselines across multiple embodiments in simulation, and runs language-conditioned bimanual manipulation on a real humanoid with high data efficiency.

why: The humanoid end of the embodiment axis, and the most explicit use of human video as robot training data at scale.

title: SAFE: Multitask Failure Detection for Vision-Language-Action Models
tldr: A generalist policy needs a generalist failure detector, and the VLA's own internal features already predict failure well enough to give one scalar.

problem.task: Detect, during execution and on unseen tasks, that a VLA policy is failing.

inputs.name: VLA internal features
inputs.chars: Read from inside OpenVLA, π₀ or π₀-FAST while it acts.

outputs.name: failure likelihood
outputs.chars: One scalar, thresholded with conformal prediction to control the alert rate.

training.supervision: Successful and failed rollouts. Evaluated on tasks held out entirely.
training.note: Generalizing across tasks is the actual problem — prior detectors were fit per task.

method.intuition: The policy already computes whether things are going well. The information is in its features, so the detector does not need its own perception stack.

datasets.name: simulated and real rollouts of OpenVLA, π₀, π₀-FAST

experiments.headline: State-of-the-art failure detection on unseen tasks with the best accuracy / detection-time trade-off, using conformal prediction for calibrated alerts.

why: The robot-side mirror of procedural mistake detection — same loop stage, different embodiment, almost no shared literature.

title: Physically Grounded Vision-Language Models for Robotic Manipulation
tldr: VLMs recognize a wine glass but do not know it is fragile. After 39.6K crowd-sourced and 417K automated physical-concept annotations, a planner that consults one picks it up differently.

problem.task: Predict physical object concepts from images, and use them inside an LLM robotic planner.

inputs.name: concept query
inputs.chars: Material, fragility, deformability, mass, transparency — including held-out concepts.

training.supervision: PhysObjects: 39.6K crowd-sourced plus 417K automated physical concept annotations.
training.note: The claim being tested is that human priors about physical properties are recoverable from appearance.

method.intuition: Physical properties are not visible, but people infer them from appearance reliably, so a VLM can learn that prior from annotations rather than from physics.
method.backbone: VLM fine-tuned on PhysObjects + LLM planner

metrics: concept prediction accuracy including held-out concepts
baselines: planners without a physically grounded VLM
experiments.headline: Better physical concept understanding including generalization to held-out concepts, improved planning, and higher real-robot task success.

why: Sits exactly on the course's title: it is the paper about physically grounding a model that otherwise only knows appearance.

title: TrackVLA: Embodied Visual Tracking in the Wild
tldr: Recognition and planning are usually separate modules that fail separately. Sharing one LLM backbone between a language head and a diffusion trajectory head makes them help each other.

problem.task: Follow a named target through a dynamic, occluding environment using only egocentric vision.

inputs.name: egocentric video
inputs.chars: Robot-mounted, severe occlusion and scene dynamics.

outputs.name: trajectory
outputs.chars: From an anchor-based diffusion head, at 10 FPS.

training.supervision: 1.7M samples from the purpose-built EVT-Bench, graded by recognition difficulty.
training.note: Real-world evaluation is included, so the sim-to-real claim is not left implicit.

method.intuition: Tracking fails when recognition and planning disagree, so give them a shared representation and let the errors correlate instead of cascade.
method.backbone: shared LLM + LM head + anchor-based diffusion head

experiments.headline: State of the art on public benchmarks zero-shot, holding up under occlusion and scene dynamics in the real world at 10 FPS.

why: A good example of a task where perception and action cannot be cleanly separated, which is the loop argument in miniature.

title: A Survey on Vision-Language-Action Models: An Action Tokenization Perspective
tldr: Every VLA is the same pipeline with a different action token — language, code, affordance, trajectory, goal state, latent, raw action, or reasoning — and that choice explains most of the differences.

problem.task: Survey of vision-language-action models organized by how the action is tokenized.

training.note: 70 pages. The taxonomy is the deliverable.

method.intuition: Apparent architectural diversity in VLAs collapses once you ask what the action token is, which makes the design space navigable.

why: The best available map of the robot-embodiment branch, and a taxonomy worth arguing with.
